projects.title: Distributed Web Crawler
projects.description:
Most crawler projects fall over the moment you try to run more than one instance — two nodes end up hitting the same domain, nobody knows who owns what, and you need a coordinator babysitting everything. I wanted to see if I could avoid that entirely, so I built a crawler where every node figures out what it should be doing on its own, using nothing but Redis for shared state and consistent hashing for domain ownership. No leader election, no consensus protocol, no single point of failure.
 Here are a few highlights of what I built:
- ***Coordination-Free Ownership:*** Each node computes domain ownership locally from consistent hashing (128 virtual nodes per physical node), so lookups run in ~2µs and the cluster keeps crawling even if Redis goes down. Rebalancing on node changes only moves 15.5% of domains, versus 83% with naive modulo hashing.
- ***Cluster-Wide Deduplication:*** Built a Redis-backed Bloom filter that stores 10 million crawled URLs in 17 MiB — about 72x smaller than keeping the raw strings — while holding a measured false-positive rate of 0.00956, just under the 0.01 target.
- ***Adaptive, Polite Crawling:*** Implemented an AIMD-based rate controller per domain instead of a fixed crawl rate. Against servers with tight limits, it held a 94% request acceptance rate where fixed-rate crawling got rejected outright (0%).
- ***Crash Recovery Without Losing the Design:*** Added a SQLite-backed durable frontier that wraps the in-memory frontier rather than reimplementing its logic, so a crash costs ~10µs per URL to recover instead of losing the queue entirely.
The whole thing runs as a 3-node Docker Compose cluster with Prometheus metrics wired in, and sits on 2,143 tests at 93.4% coverage with strict mypy across the codebase — getting the test suite that solid was honestly as much work as the crawler itself.

projects.title: AlgoLab — High-Performance Graph Algorithm Library
projects.description:
Designed a generic Algorithm[TContext, TResult] framework with PEP 695 type parameters, frozen dataclass results, and execution tracing achieving 792 tests/second throughput. Implemented 20 algorithms processing 565k+ edges/second (BFS on 50k nodes), with Dinic's max-flow delivering 40x throughput over Edmonds-Karp on parallel networks. 
 **Key Features:** 
 - ***Blazing-Fast Graph Traversal:*** BFS traversal processing 565,000+ edges/second on 50k-node directed graphs with full execution tracing, alongside Dinic's algorithm achieving 40x throughput over Edmonds-Karp on 500-path parallel flow networks (10.8ms vs 426.8ms).
 - ***High-Performance Data Structures:*** Built a Union-Find structure with path compression and union by rank achieving 0.19μs amortized find operations on 1M-element datasets, plus Binary Lifting LCA preprocessing 65k-node trees in 253ms with 3.1μs average query time.
 - ***Strict Type Safety:*** Enforced strict static typing with mypy across 7,091 lines of source code in 65 modules — zero type-ignore comments, zero errors.
 - ***Rigorous Testing:*** Created 970 automated tests (7,052 lines) covering correctness, determinism, immutability, execution metrics, and edge cases, executing the full suite in 1.2 seconds.

projects.title: Barista AI
projects.description:
Most portfolio dashboards either give you raw numbers or an AI chatbot bolted on top — rarely both working together properly. I wanted Barista AI to actually combine the two: real quantitative finance underneath (VaR, Monte Carlo, Sharpe/Sortino) with an LLM layer that can reason about what those numbers mean for your portfolio.
 Here are a few highlights of what I built:
- ***Six Agents, One Orchestrator:*** Built a multi-agent system — portfolio reader, risk analyzer, market monitor, rebalancing advisor, memory agent, and a central orchestrator tying them together — all sharing a singleton data fetcher and cache so nothing gets duplicated across requests.
- ***Data Pipeline That Doesn't Fall Over:*** Chained Finnhub, Alpha Vantage, and yfinance with automatic fallback and thread-safe rate limiting, plus batch downloads pulling 15+ tickers in a single call. The system still works with zero API keys configured — it just quietly falls back to yfinance.
- ***Real Risk Math:*** Implemented parametric, historical, and Monte Carlo VaR (10,000 simulations, vectorized in NumPy), alongside Sharpe, Sortino, CVaR, and correlation analysis — then handed those numbers to Google Gemini to generate natural-language rebalancing insights instead of just displaying charts.
- ***Live Dashboard:*** Built a 5-page React/Next.js frontend with real-time WebSocket market streaming, FRED macro indicators, coverage across 11 global indices, and currency conversion — all served as a static export directly from FastAPI, so there's no separate reverse proxy to manage.
Getting this packaged into a single Docker container and deployed on HuggingFace Spaces, with the frontend and backend both running from one process, taught me a lot about keeping deployment simple without sacrificing the multi-agent complexity underneath.

projects.title: Financial LLM Copilot
projects.description:
Macro research usually means pulling the same indicator from FRED, the World Bank, and OECD and finding out they don't quite agree with each other. I built Financial LLM Copilot to fold that whole process into a single chat interface — ask a question about any of 102 countries across 12 economic indicators and get an answer that's reconciled across sources, not just pulled from one.
 Here are a few highlights of what I built:
- ***A 7B Model Running on Free CPU Hardware:*** Fine-tuned Mistral-7B with QLoRA, quantized it to GGUF Q4_K_M (4.37GB), and served it through llama-cpp-python entirely on CPU. Getting a 7-billion parameter model to run acceptably on Hugging Face's free-tier CPU meant tuning context length, batch size, and thread count until it actually held up.
- ***Source Triangulation with Confidence Grading:*** Built a layer that reconciles FRED, World Bank, and OECD values into a consensus figure, then grades confidence (high/medium/low) based on how much the sources actually agree — so an answer comes with a sense of how trustworthy it is, not just a bare number.
- ***A Reproducible Training Pipeline:*** Instead of hand-writing training data, I built a generator that produces 4,304 instruction-tuning samples from 52 question templates and 42 curated comparison pairs, fully reproducible from a fixed seed and split into train/validation sets.
- ***Four Workspaces:*** Built out a Streamlit frontend with streaming chat, regional analysis, global rankings, and multi-country comparison, all rendered with Plotly.
Worth being upfront about: the live FRED and World Bank API clients exist in the offline data pipeline, but the deployed app currently answers from a seeded synthetic dataset behind the same data contract rather than hitting those APIs live — wiring that up end-to-end is the natural next step. What I'm most proud of here is just getting a real 7B model to run acceptably on free CPU hardware at all; nearly every design choice in the app was shaped by that constraint.

projects.title: Stock Prediction Platform
projects.description:
Most retail trading tools I looked at either backtest without realistic costs or spit out a price prediction with zero explanation of why. I built QuantEdge to close both gaps — a strategy backtester that actually models slippage, commission, and stop-loss, paired with a direction classifier that shows its reasoning instead of acting like a black box.
 Here are a few highlights of what I built:
- ***Cost-Aware Backtesting:*** Built a vectorbt-powered engine running SMA-crossover, RSI, and MACD strategies with slippage, commission, and a 5% stop-loss baked in, reporting Sharpe, max drawdown, win rate, profit factor, alpha, and beta against exchange-specific benchmarks across 31 mapped global exchanges.
- ***Explainable Predictions, Not Black-Box Ones:*** Trained an XGBoost classifier over 10 lagged technical features (all properly shift(1)'d to avoid lookahead bias), validated with 6-split expanding-window walk-forward testing instead of a naive random split. Every prediction ships with a SHAP TreeExplainer breakdown of its top 8 contributing features.
- ***Data Layer That Handles Real-World Rate Limits:*** Chained yfinance as primary with a TwelveData REST fallback behind a thread-safe token-bucket limiter, plus layered TTL caching — so the platform stays usable across 31 exchanges and 17 currencies even when a provider throttles you.
- ***One Container, Full Stack:*** Built a 15-endpoint rate-limited FastAPI backend plus a WebSocket price stream, paired with a Next.js 14 dashboard (6 routes, 71 components) that gets statically exported and served directly by the same Uvicorn process — a single Docker image, deployable to HuggingFace Spaces' single-port constraint.
The walk-forward validation and SHAP explainability were the parts I cared most about getting right — it's easy to build an ML model that looks good on a random train/test split and then falls apart on real time-series data, and I wanted to actually avoid that trap.

projects.title: Option Pricing
projects.description:
Pricing options properly means juggling a handful of different models depending on what you're actually pricing — European options don't need the same machinery as a Barrier option with early exercise. I built this platform to bring all three major pricing approaches into one place: Black-Scholes for the analytical cases, Monte Carlo simulation for path-dependent exotics, and a Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial tree for American-style early exercise.
 Here are a few highlights of what I built:
- ***Three Pricing Models, Eight Option Types:*** Implemented Black-Scholes, Monte Carlo (with antithetic variates for variance reduction), and Binomial Tree models covering European, American, Asian (arithmetic/geometric), Lookback, and Barrier options — including full Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega, Rho) computed from scratch, without relying on SciPy for the normal distribution functions.
- ***Live Global Market Data:*** Wired in a real-time options chain engine pulling from Yahoo Finance across 30+ countries and 6 regions, with historical volatility calculation, dividend yield adjustment, and risk-free rate pulled straight from 13-week Treasury data.
- ***Multi-Currency, Multi-Region:*** Built a Chart.js dashboard with live FX conversion across 8 currencies and 180+ pre-configured tickers spanning NYSE, NASDAQ, LSE, NSE, BSE, TSE, HKEX and more, plus moneyness classification (ITM/ATM/OTM) and model convergence analysis so you can sanity-check the numbers across methods.
Running this as a serverless Flask backend on Vercel, with a vanilla JS frontend and no heavy frameworks, kept the whole thing fast and simple to deploy.

projects.title: VolBench — Crypto Volatility Forecasting Benchmark
projects.description:
Most volatility-forecasting comparisons quietly assume two things: that a more complex model will win, and that the day boundary used to aggregate the data doesn't matter. I wanted to actually test both assumptions instead of assuming them, so I built VolBench to compare five forecasting models — from a naive baseline up through HAR-RV, Ridge, LightGBM, and a GRU — on crypto markets, which don't have a real market close the way equities do, and then re-ran the entire benchmark at six different daily boundaries to see if the results held up.
 **Key Features:**
 - ***A Pre-Registered Protocol, Verifiable From Git History:*** I committed and tagged the evaluation protocol before writing a single forecasting model — the tagged commit's source tree provably contains no model code, no dataset builder, and no statistics module. Anyone can check this themselves from the git log rather than taking my word for it.
 - ***Checksum-Verified Data, Measured Not Repaired:*** Ingested 1-minute klines for four crypto assets from Binance's public archives, verifying every monthly file against its SHA-256 checksum. Data quality issues (duplicates, gaps, misaligned bars) were counted and reported rather than silently cleaned up, since fixing them would change the actual forecasting target.
 - ***Statistical Testing Built From Scratch:*** Implemented Diebold-Mariano with Newey-West HAC variance and the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction, Holm-Bonferroni multiple-comparison correction, and a Hansen-Lunde-Nason Model Confidence Set with a stationary bootstrap — all from the original papers, using only NumPy and SciPy, no econometrics package doing the work for me.
 - ***Leakage Prevented Structurally:*** Fold generation lives in exactly one shared function, every model's scaler is fit only inside that model's own training fold, and a runtime guard literally refuses to evaluate the held-out period until every model's configuration is frozen.
 - ***The Actual Finding:*** Across 24 asset-boundary combinations, Ridge beat HAR-RV in 14, the GRU in 11, and LightGBM in just 1 — so more complexity didn't translate to a better model in any consistent way. And the ranking of models shifted depending on which daily boundary I used to aggregate the data, which was the whole question I set out to test.
This is a batch research pipeline, not a deployed app — there's no API, no database, no frontend. It's source code, config, and a written report. The part I'm most proud of isn't any single number; it's that the pre-registration is checkable by a stranger, and the conclusion I reported is the one the data actually gave me, not the one that would've made the project look more impressive.

projects.title: AI Fitness Coach
projects.description:
Most AI wrapper apps fall apart the moment a single API call fails. I wanted to build something that could actually survive that — a fitness coaching app where an LLM going down, a database timing out, or a rate limit getting hit doesn't take the whole thing offline. So I built AI Fitness Coach around a stack of production-grade resilience patterns most portfolio projects skip entirely.
 Here are a few highlights of what I built:
- ***Multi-Agent Orchestration with Real Fallback:*** Built 2 Langflow flows for workout and macro generation, backed by a custom OpenRouter component that chains 3 models (GLM-4.5 → DeepSeek → GPT-4o-mini) so the app keeps answering even if the free-tier model gets rate-limited or goes down.
- ***Circuit Breakers, Not Just Try/Except:*** Implemented a thread-safe circuit breaker with closed/open/half-open states protecting OpenRouter, AstraDB, and Langflow independently, plus a sliding-window rate limiter (5/min, 30/hour, 200/day per user) to stop abuse before it becomes a bill.
- ***AI Safety Guard:*** Added input filtering with 15 regex patterns to catch prompt injection and off-topic queries, and output scanning that catches unsafe dosage or exercise advice before it ever reaches the user — since a fitness app giving bad advice is a real risk, not a hypothetical one.
- ***Graceful Degradation Everywhere:*** Wrapped AstraDB with a SafeCollectionProxy that falls back to in-memory storage per call, and split Langflow into its own container so the core app stays usable on just 512MB RAM even if Langflow is down entirely.
Running this as a 4-service Docker Compose stack — Nginx handling WebSocket proxying, non-root execution, health checks, zero exposed ports — behind a Cloudflare Tunnel was where most of the infrastructure learning happened. It's not deployed to a public server yet, but the whole thing runs and holds up locally exactly as designed.

projects.title: Customer Shopping Behavior Analysis
projects.description:
An end-to-end retail analytics project built around a simple question: what actually drives customer spending, and does the data back up common assumptions about discounts and subscriptions? I took a raw dataset of 3,900 customer records through the full pipeline — cleaning, database migration, SQL analysis, and dashboarding — the way a real analytics team would.
 **Key Features:**
 - ***Careful Data Cleaning:*** Instead of filling missing review ratings with a single global average, I imputed them by category median so ratings stayed realistic within each product type. Also standardized every column to snake_case and engineered new features like age-group segmentation and a purchase-frequency-in-days mapping.
 - ***Real SQL, Not Just SELECT *:*** Migrated the cleaned data into PostgreSQL and wrote 10+ queries using CTEs and window functions (ROW_NUMBER, PARTITION BY) to rank top products per category and dig into revenue, discount effectiveness, and subscription behavior.
 - ***Customer Segmentation Logic:*** Built a New/Returning/Loyal classification straight into SQL using CASE statements based on purchase history, which is the kind of segmentation a marketing team could actually act on.
 - ***Power BI Dashboards:*** Turned the SQL output into two interactive dashboards covering customer demographics, category performance, and subscriber vs. non-subscriber spending comparisons.
It's a smaller project than some of my others, but it was a good exercise in doing the unglamorous parts of analytics properly — the cleaning and imputation decisions end up mattering just as much as the final dashboard.

projects.title: Vendor Performance Analysis
projects.description:
A supply chain analytics project built around a real question: which vendors are actually worth the relationship, and where is money getting tied up unnecessarily? I processed close to 2GB of transactional data — 12.8 million sales records and 2.4 million purchase records — across 131 vendors and over 12,000 brands to find out.
 **Key Features:**
 - ***ETL Pipeline That Actually Scales:*** Built a Python-based pipeline ingesting sales, purchases, inventory, and vendor invoice CSVs into a normalized SQLite database across 6 tables, with the full ingestion running in under 8 minutes despite the data volume.
 - ***SQL-Driven Vendor Scorecards:*** Wrote multi-table JOIN queries to build out a vendor_sales_summary table covering 10,692 brand-vendor combinations, calculating gross profit, profit margin, stock turnover, and sales-to-purchase ratios along the way.
 - ***Statistical Validation, Not Just Eyeballing Trends:*** Ran hypothesis testing (t-tests) with SciPy to actually validate whether profitability differences between vendor segments were statistically significant, rather than assuming a pattern in the data was real.
 - ***Findings With Real Business Weight:*** The analysis surfaced 198 high-margin brands that were underperforming on volume, found the top 10 vendors account for roughly 65.69% of total purchases (a real concentration risk), quantified a 72% unit cost reduction from bulk purchasing, and flagged $2.71M in working capital sitting in unsold inventory.
 - ***Power BI Dashboard:*** Turned the SQL output into an interactive dashboard so the KPIs and vendor comparisons are actually usable by someone who isn't going to open a Jupyter notebook.
This one was less about fancy modeling and more about doing the analytics fundamentals — clean ETL, proper joins, actual hypothesis testing — well enough that the numbers hold up.

projects.title: Portfolio Optimization Using Python
projects.description:
A hands-on application of Modern Portfolio Theory: given a set of ETFs, what allocation actually maximizes risk-adjusted return, and can I get there with real math instead of guesswork? I built this to optimize allocation across 5 ETFs (SPY, BND, GLD, QQQ, VTI) using 8 years of historical pricing data and a proper constrained optimization approach.
 **Key Features:**
 - ***Real Optimization, Not a Heuristic:*** Used scipy's SLSQP algorithm to solve for the weights that maximize Sharpe Ratio, with an equality constraint (weights sum to 1) and a boundary constraint capping any single asset at 40% to force diversification instead of letting the optimizer pile into one ETF.
 - ***Lognormal Returns:*** Calculated returns using log returns rather than simple arithmetic returns, since they compound more accurately and have better statistical properties for this kind of analysis.
 - ***Live Data Pipeline:*** Pulled 2,010 trading days of adjusted close prices via yfinance and the current 10-year Treasury rate via the FRED API, so the risk-free rate baseline for the Sharpe calculation isn't a stale hardcoded number.
 - ***Real Output:*** On the data pulled during this run, the optimizer landed on a portfolio with a 0.7478 Sharpe Ratio, 14.36% expected annual return, and 13.67% expected volatility — numbers that'll shift as market data updates, but the pipeline itself is what mattered here.
This was a good exercise in taking the finance theory (covariance matrices, Sharpe ratio, constrained optimization) most people just read about and actually wiring it up end-to-end with live data.

projects.title: Credit Risk Analysis
projects.description:
Built a supervised classifier on the German Credit dataset to score loan applicants as good or bad credit risk — the kind of problem where a wrong call actually costs someone money. Rather than just training one model and calling it done, I set up a proper benchmark: four tree-based classifiers under identical conditions so the comparison actually meant something.
 **Key Features:**
 - ***Controlled Model Benchmark:*** Ran Decision Tree, Random Forest, Extra Trees, and XGBoost through the same 5-fold GridSearchCV setup across 261 hyperparameter combinations on a stratified 80/20 split. XGBoost came out ahead at 67.6% test accuracy, with Extra Trees close behind at 64.8%.
 - ***Train/Serve Consistency:*** Persisted the trained model and all five fitted LabelEncoders as separate joblib artifacts, so the Streamlit app loads the exact transformers used during training instead of re-deriving encodings — a small detail that avoids a common source of bugs in deployed ML apps.
 - ***Handling Imbalance:*** The dataset skews about 70/30 toward good credit, so I applied class_weight='balanced' across the sklearn models and a computed scale_pos_weight for XGBoost rather than ignoring the skew.
 - ***Reproducible Retraining:*** Wrote a standalone retrain.py that reruns the cleaning, encoding, and grid search outside the notebook, so retraining isn't locked inside exploratory code.
 - ***Live Streamlit App:*** Built a simple interface where you plug in an applicant's details and get a real-time risk classification back.
A few honest caveats: I shipped Extra Trees instead of the better-scoring XGBoost, dropped rows with missing account data rather than imputing (which cost about half the dataset), and only tracked accuracy — recall on the 'bad risk' class would've been the more meaningful metric here. Good project for the end-to-end pipeline experience; the model performance itself has clear room to improve.

projects.title: AI Powered NIDS
projects.description:
Developed a production-grade AI-NIDS that modernizes legacy Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) into a modular, real-time intelligence platform. The system captures live network traffic, extracts complex statistical flow features aligned with industry-standard benchmarks, and employs dual-layer Machine Learning (Isolation Forest for zero-day anomalies and Random Forest for known attack patterns). 
 **Key Features:** 
 - ***Real-World Training:*** Integrated kagglehub for automated, memory-safe ingestion and training on 250,000+ records of cleaned CICIDS2017 data.
 - ***Live Observability:*** Built a responsive React/Vite dashboard featuring protocol distribution charts, live traffic volume tracking, and prioritized security alert tables.
 - ***Privacy-First Design:*** Implemented a custom IP-hashing utility on the frontend to anonymize sensitive internal addresses, making the project safe for public portfolio galleries and LinkedIn demos.
 - ***Modular Pipeline:*** Decoupled architecture with a FastAPI backend, SQLite persistence, and a standalone packet-sniffing orchestrated via background threads.
